questions.question: [Cases & Their Uses] Q: What is the function of the nominative case?
questions.correctAnswer: It marks the subject of the verb and the complement after verbs like sum (to be). For example: puella currit (the girl runs).
questions.explanation: It marks the subject of the verb and the complement after verbs like sum (to be). For example: puella currit (the girl runs).

questions.question: [Cases & Their Uses] Q: When is the vocative different from the nominative?
questions.correctAnswer: Only in the second declension masculine singular, where -us becomes -e (e.g. Marce, not Marcus) and -ius becomes -i (e.g. fili, not filius).
questions.explanation: Only in the second declension masculine singular, where -us becomes -e (e.g. Marce, not Marcus) and -ius becomes -i (e.g. fili, not filius).

questions.question: [Cases & Their Uses] Q: What is the difference between the accusative and dative cases?
questions.correctAnswer: The accusative marks the direct object (what is directly acted upon: puellam video — I see the girl). The dative marks the indirect object (to/for whom: puellae librum dedi — I gave a book to the girl).
questions.explanation: The accusative marks the direct object (what is directly acted upon: puellam video — I see the girl). The dative marks the indirect object (to/for whom: puellae librum dedi — I gave a book to the girl).

questions.question: [Narrative & Style in Prose] Q: Why is word order significant in Latin prose?
questions.correctAnswer: Latin word order is flexible, so authors place words in specific positions for emphasis. The first and last positions in a sentence are the most emphatic, and any unexpected positioning draws attention.
questions.explanation: Latin word order is flexible, so authors place words in specific positions for emphasis. The first and last positions in a sentence are the most emphatic, and any unexpected positioning draws attention.

questions.question: [Narrative & Style in Prose] Q: What is hyperbaton and what effect does it create?
questions.correctAnswer: Hyperbaton is the separation of an adjective from its noun (e.g. 'magna cum virtute' instead of 'cum magna virtute'). It draws attention to both words and creates a literary, emphasised effect.
questions.explanation: Hyperbaton is the separation of an adjective from its noun (e.g. 'magna cum virtute' instead of 'cum magna virtute'). It draws attention to both words and creates a literary, emphasised effect.

questions.question: [Narrative & Style in Prose] Q: Define tricolon and give an example.
questions.correctAnswer: A group of three parallel phrases or clauses that build emphasis and climax. The most famous example is Caesar's 'veni, vidi, vici' (I came, I saw, I conquered).
questions.explanation: A group of three parallel phrases or clauses that build emphasis and climax. The most famous example is Caesar's 'veni, vidi, vici' (I came, I saw, I conquered).

questions.question: [Nouns & Declensions] Q: How many declensions are there in Latin?
questions.correctAnswer: Five: first (a-stem), second (o-stem), third (consonant/i-stem), fourth (u-stem), and fifth (e-stem).
questions.explanation: Five: first (a-stem), second (o-stem), third (consonant/i-stem), fourth (u-stem), and fifth (e-stem).

questions.question: [Nouns & Declensions] Q: What gender are most first declension nouns? Name two masculine exceptions.
questions.correctAnswer: Mostly feminine. Masculine exceptions include nauta (sailor) and agricola (farmer).
questions.explanation: Mostly feminine. Masculine exceptions include nauta (sailor) and agricola (farmer).

questions.question: [Nouns & Declensions] Q: How do you find the stem of a third declension noun?
questions.correctAnswer: Remove the genitive singular ending (-is) from the genitive form. For example: rex, regis → stem is reg-.
questions.explanation: Remove the genitive singular ending (-is) from the genitive form. For example: rex, regis → stem is reg-.

questions.question: [Poetic Metre & Style] Q: What is a dactylic hexameter and which types of poetry use it?
questions.correctAnswer: A line of six feet, each foot being a dactyl (- uu) or spondee (--), with a spondee or trochee in the final foot. It is the metre of epic poetry (Virgil's Aeneid, Ovid's Metamorphoses).
questions.explanation: A line of six feet, each foot being a dactyl (- uu) or spondee (--), with a spondee or trochee in the final foot. It is the metre of epic poetry (Virgil's Aeneid, Ovid's Metamorphoses).

questions.question: [Poetic Metre & Style] Q: What is the caesura and why is it important?
questions.correctAnswer: A natural pause within a hexameter line, usually in the third foot. It divides the line into two parts and allows the poet to structure meaning within the metrical framework.
questions.explanation: A natural pause within a hexameter line, usually in the third foot. It divides the line into two parts and allows the poet to structure meaning within the metrical framework.

questions.question: [Poetic Metre & Style] Q: Explain elision with an example.
questions.correctAnswer: When a word ending in a vowel or -m is followed by a word beginning with a vowel or h-, the final syllable is not pronounced separately. Example: multum ille et terris becomes multill'et terris.
questions.explanation: When a word ending in a vowel or -m is followed by a word beginning with a vowel or h-, the final syllable is not pronounced separately. Example: multum ille et terris becomes multill'et terris.
